title: Kiddush
hook: a cup of wine or grape juice declares the day holy, remembering creation and the Exodus

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing the children: Ephraim and Manasseh, the four mothers, and hands resting on a head. Your line was hands on heads. Day one hundred two.

At a wedding, there's a moment when someone taps a glass, everyone stands, and a toast turns an ordinary evening into an occasion. Same room, same people. But now it's official: this night matters. On Friday night, in Jewish homes all over the world, there's a moment like that at the table. Someone lifts a full cup of wine or grape juice, the room gets quiet, and they say words that turn a Friday evening into something else. Today: Kiddush.
screen: `SOMEONE TAPS A GLASS.` → `NOW IT'S OFFICIAL.` → `A FULL CUP ON FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kiddush means making holy, from the same root as kadosh, holy. It comes from the commandment, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The rabbis asked: how do you remember a day? And they answered: you say so, out loud, over a cup of wine. Wine, because it's what people drink at a celebration. Grape juice works too, and many families use it. If there's no wine at all, the blessing can be said over the challah. On Friday night, Kiddush begins with the last lines of the creation story in Genesis: "And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Then God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. Then comes the blessing over the fruit of the vine, and then a longer blessing that names two reasons for the day. Shabbat is a remembrance of creation, the world God made and finished. And it's a reminder of the Exodus, leaving Egypt. Why the Exodus? Because in Deuteronomy the Sabbath commandment says: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. Slaves don't get days off. Free people do. So every Friday night, one cup holds two memories: the world was made, and we were set free. Customs vary. Some stand, some sit. Some hold the cup in the palm of the hand. Afterward, everyone takes a sip, often from little cups poured from the big one. It's short, maybe a minute. But it does what the toast does at a wedding. It says it out loud: this time is different.
screen: `KIDDUSH: MAKING HOLY.` · `REMEMBER IT OVER WINE.` · `CREATION, AND LEAVING EGYPT.` · `FREE PEOPLE REST.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY, TO KEEP IT HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: raise any drink and say one sentence of thanks. Water is fine. Coffee is fine. Pick up whatever is near you, or picture it. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that you didn't make but get to enjoy, and one way you're more free than you once were. Then lift the cup a little, and say one sentence of thanks, out loud if you can. If you pray, you can offer it to God. Then drink slowly. The bell holds the time.
Kiddush. Making holy: a blessing over wine or grape juice that declares Shabbat holy, remembering creation and the Exodus.
Your line: make it holy out loud. Today, before one meal or one moment, say out loud that it matters, even in one sentence. Day one hundred two.

howItsDone: On Friday night, before the meal, someone at the table lifts a cup of wine or grape juice and recites Kiddush, beginning with Genesis 2:1–3, and everyone then takes a sip.
